lessons.title: Letters, words and capitals
objectives: Recognize the main patterns in letters, words and capitals.
Apply these patterns to a fresh example and explain a correction.
lessons.explanation: English uses 26 letters. Each letter has an upper-case and lower-case form. A letter is a written symbol; several letters can form a word. Begin a statement with a capital and finish it with a full stop. A person’s name also starts with a capital. A capital changes the written form, not the word’s meaning.
lessons.explanationBn: বাক্যের শুরুতে বড় হাতের অক্ষর এবং শেষে পূর্ণচ্ছেদ ব্যবহার করো।
examples: a → A; m → M; t → T. These pairs show the same letters.
A book. The word book has four letters.
We read. W begins the statement with a capital.
lessons.incorrect: we read
lessons.correct: We read.

guided.prompt: Write the capital form of m.
guided.explanation: M is the upper-case form of m.

independent.prompt: Put these letters in order to spell a familiar object: b o o k.
independent.explanation: Book is spelt b-o-o-k.

quiz.prompt: Which statement begins correctly?
quiz.explanation: A sentence starts with a capital.

quiz.prompt: B and b represent the same letter.
quiz.explanation: Upper and lower case are two written forms.

lessons.title: Who does what?
objectives: Recognize the main patterns in who does what?.
Apply these patterns to a fresh example and explain a correction.
lessons.explanation: A basic statement usually names a subject and gives it a finite verb. The subject tells us who or what the statement is about. The verb gives an action or a state. Some verbs need an object or complement. A group such as near the door names a place but does not make a complete statement.
lessons.explanationBn: Subject হলো কার বা কিসের কথা বলা হচ্ছে; verb দিয়ে কাজ বা অবস্থা বোঝানো হয়।
examples: Birds sing. Birds is the subject; sing is the verb.
The room is quiet. Is links the room to a description.
I read a message. A message is the object of read.
lessons.incorrect: In the garden.
lessons.correct: The children play in the garden.

guided.prompt: Which word gives the action in Students write notes?
guided.explanation: Write tells us what the students do.

independent.prompt: Order these words; include a full stop: books / read / We
independent.explanation: A common statement order is subject + verb + object.

quiz.prompt: Which is a complete statement?
quiz.explanation: The lesson is a subject and starts is a finite verb.

quiz.prompt: The ___ is blue. Choose: sky / walks
quiz.explanation: Sky names the thing being described.

lessons.title: Base, past and participle forms
objectives: Recognize the main patterns in base, past and participle forms.
Apply these patterns to a fresh example and explain a correction.
lessons.explanation: Regular past forms and past participles usually end in -ed. A final e normally takes -d; consonant + y normally becomes -ied. Irregular verbs have forms that must be learned in context. A past participle combines with have in perfect constructions and be in passive constructions. Do not assume that every past form is also the participle. Use a dictionary’s verb table when unsure.
examples: walk → walked → walked; live → lived → lived.
study → studied → studied; consonant + y changes to i.
go → went → gone; write → wrote → written.
Yesterday I wrote a note. I have written three notes.
lessons.incorrect: She has went home.
lessons.correct: She has gone home.

guided.explanation: Learned is a regular past form.

independent.prompt: She has ___ the email. (write)
independent.explanation: Have/has takes the past participle written.

quiz.prompt: Write the past form of study.
quiz.explanation: Consonant + y changes to i before -ed.

quiz.prompt: Choose the past form of go.
quiz.explanation: Went is the simple past; gone is the participle.

lessons.title: Capitals for names and sentence beginnings
objectives: Recognize the main patterns in capitals for names and sentence beginnings.
Apply these patterns to a fresh example and explain a correction.
lessons.explanation: Capitalize the first word of a sentence and the pronoun I. Proper names identify a particular person, place, organization or product; common nouns usually stay lower case. Days, months, named holidays, languages and nationalities take capitals. Seasons usually do not. Titles of works follow a chosen style; do not capitalize every ordinary noun in a paragraph. In letters, capitalize the beginning of the salutation and the first word of the closing.
examples: We study English on Monday. Language and day take capitals.
The meeting is in November, during autumn. Month is capitalized; season is not.
I visited Dhaka. The pronoun and city name take capitals.
lessons.incorrect: we study english on monday.
lessons.correct: We study English on Monday.

guided.explanation: Names of months take capitals.

independent.prompt: Write the pronoun i correctly.
independent.explanation: The pronoun I is always capitalized.

quiz.prompt: Choose the corrected sentence.
quiz.explanation: Language names are proper names.

quiz.prompt: All common nouns need capital letters.
quiz.explanation: Ordinary common nouns usually stay lower case.

lessons.title: Build a personal spelling routine
objectives: Recognize the main patterns in build a personal spelling routine.
Apply these patterns to a fresh example and explain a correction.
lessons.explanation: Check an unfamiliar word in a reliable dictionary and notice its spelling, meaning and pronunciation. Keep a personal list of your own errors rather than copying thousands of words without review. Group related subject words and confused pairs. Practise a short basic list, cover the answer, write from memory, then check. Use each corrected word in a fresh sentence. Electronic tools can suggest corrections, but a correctly spelt wrong word can escape them. Revisit difficult words across several sessions.
examples: necessary: one c and two s letters. I packed the necessary forms.
separate: notice a after the first r. Keep a separate notebook.
receive: notice ei after c in this word. I receive updates by email.
lessons.incorrect: I recieve the message.
lessons.correct: I receive the message.

guided.explanation: Separate has a after the first r.

independent.prompt: Correct the spelling: neccessary
independent.explanation: Necessary has one c and two s letters.

quiz.prompt: Correct: recieve
quiz.explanation: Receive uses ei after c.

quiz.prompt: A spelling checker always notices a correctly spelt word used with the wrong meaning.
quiz.explanation: Context can require a different word even when spelling is valid.

lessons.title: Find the subject before choosing a verb
objectives: Recognize the main patterns in find the subject before choosing a verb.
Apply these patterns to a fresh example and explain a correction.
lessons.explanation: In the present simple, a third-person singular subject generally takes an -s or -es verb. A plural subject generally takes the base form. Intervening phrases do not change the subject: the box of pencils is singular. Subjects joined by and are usually plural. Everyone and each normally take singular verbs. In sentences beginning with there, find the subject after the verb. With or/nor, match the nearer subject when number differs; rephrasing can improve clarity.
examples: The list of topics is useful. List is the subject.
The learners and the tutor meet weekly. And joins two subjects.
Everyone has a notebook. Everyone is singular.
There are two chairs by the door. Chairs is plural.
lessons.incorrect: The group of students are ready.
lessons.correct: The group of students is ready. (The group is treated as one unit.)

guided.explanation: Basket, rather than apples, controls the verb.

independent.prompt: Each learner ___ a pen. (has/have)
independent.explanation: Each learner is singular.

quiz.prompt: There ___ three tasks today.
quiz.explanation: Three tasks is the plural subject.

quiz.prompt: My friends and I ___ together.
quiz.explanation: A compound subject including I takes study.

lessons.title: Numbers, dates and clear abbreviations
objectives: Recognize the main patterns in numbers, dates and clear abbreviations.
Apply these patterns to a fresh example and explain a correction.
lessons.explanation: Number style depends on the writing context. Use a consistent house style: small nontechnical numbers are often written as words, while measurements, statistics and dates commonly use numerals. Rewrite a sentence to avoid starting it with a long numeral. A date written as 12 May 2026 avoids numeric date-order ambiguity. Spell out an unfamiliar abbreviation at first mention and place its short form in parentheses. Avoid informal text-message abbreviations in formal requests.
examples: We need three volunteers. A small nontechnical number is written out.
The sample weighed 12 kg. A measurement uses a numeral and unit.
Please reply by 12 May 2026. The month name avoids date ambiguity.
The quality review team (QRT) meets today. QRT appears after its full form.
lessons.incorrect: Plz send 2 files asap.
lessons.correct: Please send the two files as soon as possible.

guided.prompt: Which date is least ambiguous internationally?
guided.explanation: The named month makes the intended date clear.

independent.prompt: Rewrite for a formal email: Plz send 3 copies asap.
independent.explanation: Review the structure, accuracy and meaning rather than matching a fixed model.
rubric: Task fulfilled with a clear meaning

quiz.explanation: Measurements and statistics often use numerals; follow the relevant style.

quiz.prompt: How should an unfamiliar abbreviation first appear?
options: Full expression followed by the short form
answers: Full expression followed by the short form
quiz.explanation: Define unfamiliar abbreviations for readers.

lessons.title: Possession, contractions and ordinary plurals
objectives: Recognize the main patterns in possession, contractions and ordinary plurals.
Apply these patterns to a fresh example and explain a correction.
lessons.explanation: A contraction uses an apostrophe for omitted letters: do not becomes don't. A singular noun normally forms possession with apostrophe + s. A regular plural already ending in s adds only an apostrophe; an irregular plural such as children adds apostrophe + s. Ordinary plurals take no apostrophe. Possessive pronouns such as hers, ours and its do not take apostrophes. It's means it is or it has. Style guides differ over some singular names ending in s; follow a consistent style.
examples: The learner's desk: one learner owns or uses it.
The learners' desks: several learners.
The children's books: irregular plural possession.
The cat moved its tail. It's restless: it is restless.
lessons.incorrect: The students book's are on the table.
lessons.correct: The students' books are on the table. (Books belonging to several students.)

guided.prompt: Write the contraction of do not.
guided.explanation: The apostrophe replaces the missing o.

independent.prompt: Complete for books belonging to several girls: the ___ books.
independent.explanation: A regular plural ending in s adds an apostrophe.

quiz.prompt: Which means it is?
quiz.explanation: It's is a contraction; its shows possession.

quiz.prompt: Choose the ordinary plural.
quiz.explanation: A regular plural takes s without an apostrophe.

lessons.title: Quoting speech accurately
objectives: Recognize the main patterns in quoting speech accurately.
Apply these patterns to a fresh example and explain a correction.
lessons.explanation: Quotation marks show words presented as direct speech. Put a speaker tag before or after the quoted speech. In the convention used here, a comma introduces the speech after a tag, and a comma replaces its final full stop when a following tag continues the sentence. A question mark belongs inside the quotation if the quoted words form a question. Single and double quotation conventions vary by style and region; be consistent. Short-work titles can take quotation marks; do not use them merely for emphasis.
examples: She said, “The room is open.” A tag introduces the quoted statement.
“The room is open,” she said. A comma links speech to the following tag.
“Is the room open?” she asked. The question mark belongs to the spoken question.
lessons.incorrect: She said The room is open.
lessons.correct: She said, “The room is open.”

guided.prompt: What do quotation marks identify here?
guided.explanation: They mark the quoted words, not general emphasis.

independent.prompt: Punctuate this direct speech with a consistent quotation style: Is the bus here she asked
independent.explanation: Review the structure, accuracy and meaning rather than matching a fixed model.
rubric: Task fulfilled with a clear meaning

quiz.explanation: A comma separates the quoted statement from the following speaker tag.

quiz.prompt: A question mark for quoted speech goes inside its quotation marks.

examples: Your folder is here.

lessons.title: Simple, compound, complex and compound-complex
objectives: Recognize the main patterns in simple, compound, complex and compound-complex.
Apply these patterns to a fresh example and explain a correction.
lessons.explanation: A simple sentence has one independent clause. A compound sentence connects at least two independent clauses, often with a comma and a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so). A complex sentence contains an independent clause and at least one dependent clause. A compound-complex sentence has at least two independent clauses and a dependent clause. A dependent clause introduced by because, although or when cannot stand alone here. Vary sentence length to make the relationship between ideas clear.
examples: The rain stopped. One independent clause: simple.
The rain stopped, so we left. Two independent clauses: compound.
When the rain stopped, we left. A dependent clause plus a main clause: complex.
When the rain stopped, we left, and the guide followed. Two main clauses plus a dependent clause: compound-complex.
lessons.incorrect: Because the library closed.
lessons.correct: Because the library closed, we studied at home.

guided.prompt: Identify: The room was small, but it was comfortable.
guided.explanation: Both sides can stand alone; but joins them.

independent.prompt: Combine The bus was late and We walked using because.
independent.explanation: Put the cause in a dependent clause.

Original cause and result retained
Correct capitalization and punctuation

lessons.title: Repairing run-ons without losing meaning
objectives: Recognize the main patterns in repairing run-ons without losing meaning.
Apply these patterns to a fresh example and explain a correction.
lessons.explanation: Two independent clauses need a legitimate boundary. A comma alone creates a comma splice; no boundary creates a fused sentence. You can use a full stop, a semicolon, or a comma with an appropriate coordinating conjunction. Subordination can show why or when something happened. However is a transition, not a coordinating conjunction: use a full stop or semicolon before it when it joins two main clauses. Choose a repair that preserves the writer’s intended relationship.
examples: The gate closed. We waited outside. Two statements.
The gate closed; we waited outside. Closely related clauses.
The gate closed, so we waited outside. A result.
Because the gate closed, we waited outside. A reason.
lessons.incorrect: I finished the form, I sent it.
lessons.correct: I finished the form, and I sent it.

guided.explanation: A semicolon can join related independent clauses.

lessons.title: Put a modifier beside its meaning
objectives: Recognize the main patterns in put a modifier beside its meaning.
Apply these patterns to a fresh example and explain a correction.
lessons.explanation: A modifier adds detail to another word or phrase. Its position tells readers what it describes. Put only near the word it limits. Put descriptive phrases beside the intended noun. An awkwardly placed phrase can accidentally describe a different person or object. Test a rewrite by asking who has the described quality. Several rewrites may be correct when they clearly preserve the intended meaning.
examples: We served soup to the guests in blue bowls. This wrongly suggests guests in bowls.
We served soup in blue bowls to the guests. The bowls contain soup.
Only I reviewed the draft. Nobody else reviewed it.
I reviewed only the draft. I reviewed no other document.

lessons.correct: She drove the children to school almost every day. (The frequency is nearly every day.)

lessons.title: Give introductory actions a clear subject
objectives: Recognize the main patterns in give introductory actions a clear subject.
Apply these patterns to a fresh example and explain a correction.
lessons.explanation: An introductory modifying phrase usually describes the subject of the following main clause. If the subject cannot do the opening action, the phrase dangles. Name the actual doer immediately after the phrase, or rewrite the introduction as a full clause with its own subject. Check both grammar and logic. The purpose of a correction is to show who did what, rather than merely moving punctuation.
examples: After checking the figures, the analyst sent the report. The analyst checked.
While walking home, I noticed a new café. I was walking.
After I checked the figures, the report was sent. The full opening clause names its doer.

lessons.title: Six useful jobs for commas
objectives: Recognize the main patterns in six useful jobs for commas.
Apply these patterns to a fresh example and explain a correction.
lessons.explanation: Commas separate items in a series; the final serial comma depends on style. They often follow introductory clauses or longer phrases. A pair encloses nonessential interrupting information. A comma normally precedes a coordinating conjunction joining two independent clauses. Speaker tags use commas with quoted statements. Everyday dates, addresses and greetings can also need commas, depending on layout and convention. Do not place a comma between a simple subject and its verb or use one alone to join two main clauses.
examples: We packed pens, paper, and a notebook. A series.
After the meeting ended, we left. An introductory clause.
My bike, which is quite old, still works. A nonessential interruption.
I called, but nobody answered. Two complete clauses.
“I agree,” she said. A speech tag.
Dear Admissions Team, introduces a formal greeting in one common convention.

lessons.correct: The student writes daily.

guided.explanation: The comma follows the complete introductory clause.

lessons.title: A clear formal email or full-block letter
objectives: Recognize the main patterns in a clear formal email or full-block letter.
Apply these patterns to a fresh example and explain a correction.
lessons.explanation: Choose a polite, direct tone and a useful subject line. A full-block letter aligns its parts to the left: date, receiver details, salutation, subject if used, opening, body, closing and signature. Separate paragraphs with space and keep normal margins. An email uses receiver and subject fields rather than duplicating the postal layout. Identify your purpose early, give relevant details and make a specific request. Use appropriate titles when known; a role-based greeting is suitable when a name is unknown. Prefer clear modern expressions to elaborate outdated formulas.
examples: Subject: Request for a project meeting. Dear Project Coordinator, I am writing to request a meeting about my draft.
Could we meet on Tuesday afternoon? I can also attend at a time that suits you.
Thank you for considering my request. Kind regards, [Your name]. Brackets here mark a field you must replace.

lessons.title: Permission, absence and academic requests
objectives: Recognize the main patterns in permission, absence and academic requests.
Apply these patterns to a fresh example and explain a correction.
lessons.explanation: A request should identify the action you want, explain why it is reasonable and supply enough information for a decision. For an absence, state the relevant date and give a concise explanation without unnecessary private detail. Acknowledge missed work and propose a practical next step. For permission, specify what, when and for how long. In an academic email, use a meaningful subject line and avoid text-message abbreviations or demands. Check dates, attachments and tone before sending.
examples: Subject: Permission to use the meeting room. I would like to reserve the room from 2 pm to 3 pm on Thursday for a group discussion.
I was unable to attend the session on Monday because I was unwell. Could you advise me how to catch up on the work?
I have attached my outline. Could you please confirm whether the proposed topic is suitable?

guided.explanation: Specific information allows the recipient to decide.

lessons.title: Colons, semicolons, dashes and brackets
objectives: Recognize the main patterns in colons, semicolons, dashes and brackets.
Apply these patterns to a fresh example and explain a correction.
lessons.explanation: A colon can introduce a list or explanation after a complete clause. A semicolon can join closely related independent clauses, and can separate complex list items containing commas. A dash can mark a strong interruption or explanation; parentheses enclose less central information. A hyphen joins elements within some compound words and compound modifiers, especially before a noun. Do not treat a hyphen as a sentence-level dash. Select punctuation for the relationship you intend, and avoid adding marks without a grammatical purpose.
examples: We need three items: a pen, a ruler, and paper. The colon follows a complete clause.
The first plan failed; the second worked. Related independent clauses.
The report (attached below) explains the change. Extra information.
A well-planned route saves time. The hyphen joins a modifier before a noun.

lessons.correct: The items include pens and paper.

lessons.title: A position supported by reasons
objectives: Recognize the main patterns in a position supported by reasons.
Apply these patterns to a fresh example and explain a correction.
lessons.explanation: An academic argument links a claim to reasons and relevant evidence. A thesis states the essay’s controlling position, rather than merely announcing a topic. A useful thesis is specific enough to discuss and defensible with reasons. Distinguish opinion from evidence and ask whether a source, comparison or example really supports the claim. Avoid inventing statistics. Acknowledge uncertainty when evidence is limited and express disagreement courteously. Shared goals can establish common ground before viewpoints diverge.
examples: Topic only: Public libraries. Position: Public libraries should extend weekend hours to support working learners.
Reason: Some learners cannot attend on weekdays. Possible evidence to seek: actual opening hours and a survey of local users.
Weak: This essay discusses transport. Stronger: The city should prioritize reliable buses before expanding central parking.

lessons.correct: Longer opening hours may improve access for learners who work on weekdays; local demand should be investigated.

lessons.title: From introduction to conclusion
objectives: Recognize the main patterns in from introduction to conclusion.
Apply these patterns to a fresh example and explain a correction.
lessons.explanation: An introduction uses a relevant opening, gives enough background and states the thesis. Each body paragraph develops a focused point, often signalled by a topic sentence, then supports it with explanation and appropriate examples or evidence. A counterargument represents a reasonable opposing view fairly. A response or refutation explains why your position still holds, perhaps with a qualification. The conclusion brings the reasoning together, restates the thesis in fresh language and may offer a justified suggestion. It should not introduce an unrelated major argument.
examples: Opening: Many commuters depend on buses each day. Background: Services on the outer routes are infrequent. Thesis: Improving reliability should be the first transport priority.
Topic sentence: Reliable buses help workers plan their journeys. Explanation: Predictable arrivals reduce uncertainty. Evidence to collect: measured waiting times.
Conclusion idea: Prioritizing reliability would make existing services more useful; a small trial could test the proposal.
lessons.incorrect: Public transport matters. Another unrelated fact is that oceans are deep.
lessons.correct: Public transport matters because reliable services connect residents to daily work and study.

lessons.title: Counterarguments, refutation and revision
objectives: Recognize the main patterns in counterarguments, refutation and revision.
Apply these patterns to a fresh example and explain a correction.
lessons.explanation: Plan an argumentative essay by selecting a focused topic, brainstorming reasons and objections, and grouping related ideas. Represent a serious opposing view fairly. A refutation responds with reasoning or evidence instead of insulting its supporters. Sometimes qualifying your original position is more convincing than rejecting every objection. Revise first for structure, missing evidence and paragraph order; then edit grammar, vocabulary, spelling and punctuation. A finished argument should make clear what you claim, why, what an informed reader might object to and how you respond.
examples: Claim: A shared study room should remain open later. Reason: Evening learners need a quiet place.
Objection: Longer hours may raise staffing costs. Fair response: Begin with two evenings and evaluate actual demand and cost.
Revision question: Does each paragraph advance the thesis, and is each factual claim supported?
lessons.incorrect: Anyone who disagrees is foolish.
lessons.correct: Some readers may worry about cost; a limited trial could establish whether the benefit justifies it.
